maturityProgression.description: A composite operational health view exists, combining signals across quality, capacity, and risk.

maturityProgression.name: Managed
maturityProgression.description: Operational health is reviewed on a standing cadence and used to trigger action before failure.

maturityProgression.name: Adaptive
maturityProgression.description: The health model itself is refined as new failure modes and signals are discovered.

whatBreaksWhenWeak: Deterioration compounds quietly across functions until it becomes a visible, expensive failure.
Leadership is reassured by individually green metrics that don't reflect the whole picture.
Response to real problems is always reactive because nothing surfaced them early.
Cross-functional root causes go undiagnosed because each function only monitors its own slice.
resources.whenToUse: For any system, product, or process where failure would be costly, customer-facing, or hard to detect from a single metric.
resources.whenNotToUse: Overkill for a low-stakes process where a single metric already tells the whole story.
howToBuild: Identify the handful of signals — quality, capacity, risk, customer, financial — that together indicate system health.
Combine them into a single composite view rather than reviewing each in isolation.
Set explicit thresholds for what triggers a closer look or an intervention.
Review the composite view on a standing cadence, not only after something breaks.
howToGovern: Assign a cross-functional owner for the health view so it isn't captured by a single function's perspective.
Revisit which signals belong in the model as new failure modes are discovered.
howToMeasure: Time between actual degradation starting and it being detected by the health view.
Number of significant incidents that the health view failed to anticipate.
Frequency the health view is actually reviewed versus scheduled.
operatorQuestions: If this system were quietly degrading, how would we know before a customer told us?
Where are we compensating for a health issue with heroics instead of fixing it?
What would an early warning of deterioration actually look like here?

investigate: Ask leadership to describe how they'd currently know if this system were degrading — before a failure.
Review the last significant incident and identify what signal, if any, could have caught it earlier.
evidence: Current dashboards or reports touching quality, capacity, and risk for this system.
History of past incidents and how they were first detected.
observe: Whether health is discussed proactively or only after something breaks.
Whether different functions' views of health actually agree.
measure: Detection lag between actual degradation and it being noticed.
Coverage: what percentage of past incidents the current view would have caught.
doNotYet: Don't build an elaborate health score before confirming which signals actually predicted past failures.
Don't treat a green individual metric as proof the whole system is healthy.

healthy: A cross-functional health view is reviewed on a standing cadence and prompts real discussion.
warning: Individual metrics look fine while informal complaints about the system are increasing.
failure: A serious problem is discovered only through a customer complaint or public incident.

resources.title: Data Quality
resources.question: If two people pulled this number independently right now, would they get the same answer?
resources.whatItIs: The accuracy, consistency, and trustworthiness of the data feeding operational metrics and decisions, treated as something actively maintained rather than assumed.
resources.whyThisExists: Data degrades by default — systems change, definitions drift, manual entry introduces error. Quality has to be actively maintained, or the numbers built on top of it quietly stop meaning what they used to.
resources.whyItMatters: No amount of dashboard design or KPI architecture matters if the underlying data can't be trusted — bad inputs make sophisticated reporting actively misleading rather than merely useless.
resources.goodLooksLike: Core metrics have a single source of truth, a documented definition, and an owner accountable for their accuracy.
resources.badLooksLike: Numbers are quietly patched by hand before reporting, and everyone has learned to privately distrust the official dashboard.
failureSymptoms: Different teams report different numbers for what should be the same metric.
Data quality issues are common knowledge internally but never actually get fixed.
Reports require manual correction before anyone will trust them.
A number is quietly "adjusted" before being shared upward.
commonFailureModes: Building new dashboards on top of data nobody has verified is accurate.
Fixing a data error once without addressing the process that keeps producing it.
Allowing the same metric to have different definitions in different systems.

maturityProgression.name: Reactive
maturityProgression.description: Data quality issues are discovered incidentally and patched ad hoc when noticed.

maturityProgression.name: Repeatable
maturityProgression.description: Known data issues are common knowledge but nobody is accountable for fixing them.

maturityProgression.name: Defined
maturityProgression.description: Core metrics have a documented definition and a single source of truth.

maturityProgression.name: Managed
maturityProgression.description: Data quality is actively monitored, with known issues tracked and resolved on a cadence.

maturityProgression.name: Adaptive
maturityProgression.description: Data quality is itself a measured, continuously improved capability, not a one-time cleanup.

whatBreaksWhenWeak: Every downstream metric, dashboard, and decision inherits the same underlying distrust.
Meetings get spent debating whose number is right instead of deciding what to do.
Leadership loses confidence in data broadly, including in metrics that are actually reliable.
Automated decisions or alerts built on bad data actively cause harm rather than helping.
resources.whenToUse: Before building any new metric, dashboard, or automated decision on top of existing data.
resources.whenNotToUse: Not worth heavy investment for a metric that's about to be retired or was only ever meant to be a one-time analysis.
howToBuild: Identify the single source of truth for each core metric and eliminate competing versions.
Document how each metric is defined and calculated.
Assign an owner accountable for that metric's ongoing accuracy.
Track known data quality issues to resolution instead of routing around them.
howToGovern: Require any new metric or dashboard to reference an established source of truth before launch.
Review known data quality issues on a standing cadence until they're actually resolved.
howToMeasure: Number of known, unresolved data quality issues.
Frequency of manual correction required before reporting.
Number of competing definitions for the same nominal metric.
operatorQuestions: Where does this number actually come from, and who owns its accuracy?
What would it take for people to trust this data enough to act on it without double-checking?
Where do two systems disagree about the same fact?

investigate: Pick a core metric and trace it back to its original data source, noting every manual step along the way.
Ask two different teams to each pull the same metric independently and compare results.
evidence: Recent instances of conflicting numbers for the same metric.
Any documentation of how the metric is calculated.
History of manual corrections applied before reporting.
observe: Where people quietly adjust a number before sharing it.
Where a known data issue has persisted without anyone assigned to fix it.
measure: Rate of discrepancy between independently pulled values for the same metric.
Time known issues remain open before resolution.
doNotYet: Don't build a new dashboard on data whose quality hasn't been verified.
Don't patch a bad number once without fixing the process that produced it.

healthy: Two people pulling the same metric independently get the same answer.
warning: A number requires manual correction before anyone will present it.
failure: People have quietly stopped trusting the official dashboard altogether.

resources.title: Root Cause Analysis
resources.question: Is this actually where the failure began, or just where it became visible?
resources.whatItIs: The disciplined practice of tracing a symptom back to the system condition that produced it, rather than stopping at the first plausible explanation.
resources.whyThisExists: The place a failure appears is rarely the place it began. Root cause analysis exists because the natural stopping point — the first plausible explanation — is usually a symptom, not a cause.
resources.whyItMatters: Without root cause discipline, organizations repeatedly treat symptoms — training, tooling, headcount — while the underlying system condition keeps producing new symptoms.
resources.goodLooksLike: Investigations continue past the first obvious answer, gather evidence before concluding, and produce fixes aimed at the system, not just the incident.
resources.badLooksLike: Every investigation ends at "someone made a mistake," and the corrective action is a reminder email or a new mandatory training.
failureSymptoms: The same category of incident recurs despite previous "fixes."
Investigations conclude with an individual's error rather than a system condition.
A fix is proposed before the cause is actually confirmed with evidence.
Corrective actions are always aimed at behavior, never at the process or design.
commonFailureModes: Stopping analysis at the first cause that is politically convenient.
Confusing the first person to notice the failure with the origin of the failure.
Prescribing a solution before validating the diagnosis with evidence.

maturityProgression.name: Reactive
maturityProgression.description: Investigations stop at the first plausible explanation, usually individual error.

maturityProgression.name: Repeatable
maturityProgression.description: Some investigations dig deeper, but it depends on who happens to be involved.

maturityProgression.name: Defined
maturityProgression.description: A defined process is used to investigate significant incidents and trace them to a system cause.

maturityProgression.name: Managed
maturityProgression.description: Root cause findings are tracked, and fixes are verified to actually address the system condition.

maturityProgression.name: Adaptive
maturityProgression.description: Root cause analysis is routine for minor issues too, not reserved for major incidents.

whatBreaksWhenWeak: The same failure recurs, at full cost, because only its symptom was ever treated.
Trust erodes when "fixes" repeatedly fail to prevent recurrence.
Blame concentrates on individuals for what are actually system failures.
Improvement effort is spent addressing the wrong layer of the problem entirely.
resources.whenToUse: Any time a problem recurs, or a single incident is costly enough to warrant understanding it fully before responding.
resources.whenNotToUse: Overkill for a genuinely isolated, low-cost, non-recurring issue — proportion the investigation to the stakes.
howToBuild: When an incident occurs, ask "why" past the first answer until you reach a system condition, not a person.
Gather evidence before concluding a cause — don't let the most available explanation win by default.
Confirm the proposed root cause actually explains prior instances of the same symptom, not just this one.
Aim the fix at the system condition, and verify it actually prevents recurrence.
howToGovern: Require significant incidents to produce a documented root cause, not just a resolution.
Track whether previously "fixed" root causes actually stopped producing the symptom.
howToMeasure: Recurrence rate for previously investigated issues.
Percentage of investigations that conclude at a system cause versus an individual one.
Time from incident to a verified, evidence-based root cause.
operatorQuestions: What evidence supports that diagnosis?
What evidence would prove us wrong?
If we fix only this symptom, what system condition remains untouched?

investigate: Take the last recurring problem and ask "why" five times, testing each answer against evidence.
Check whether the last proposed fix for this issue actually prevented it from recurring.
evidence: Incident history for this type of failure.
Previous corrective actions and whether they held.
Process and system documentation relevant to where the failure occurred.
observe: Whether investigations stop at "who" instead of continuing to "why."
Whether the same fix keeps getting proposed for recurring versions of the same problem.
measure: Recurrence rate after a fix is implemented.
Time from symptom to verified system-level cause.
doNotYet: Don't propose a fix before the cause is confirmed with evidence.
Don't accept "human error" as a root cause without asking what let the error reach the customer.

healthy: Investigations routinely continue past the first plausible explanation.
warning: The same category of incident starts recurring more frequently despite previous fixes.
failure: Every incident investigation ends with blaming an individual.

resources.title: Continuous Improvement
resources.question: What was the baseline before we called this an improvement?
resources.whatItIs: The deliberate, ongoing practice of measuring a baseline, testing changes against it, and standardizing what works — as opposed to sporadic, opinion-driven fixes.
resources.whyThisExists: Without a baseline and a deliberate test, "we improved it" is a claim, not a fact. Continuous improvement exists to make that claim verifiable, repeatedly, as a standing practice.
resources.whyItMatters: Improvement without a baseline is opinion. Without a consistent improvement discipline, organizations lurch between neglect and overcorrection, and gains from past improvements erode unnoticed.
resources.goodLooksLike: Improvement work starts from a measured baseline, tests changes deliberately, and locks in gains through updated standards and governance.
resources.badLooksLike: Improvement happens in bursts after something breaks badly enough to get leadership's attention, then fades until the next crisis.
failureSymptoms: An improvement is declared successful with no baseline to compare against.
Improvement initiatives never get standardized into the actual process afterward.
The gains from a past improvement have quietly eroded and nobody noticed.
Improvement work only happens as a reaction to a crisis.
commonFailureModes: Declaring victory on an improvement with no baseline to compare against.
Running improvement initiatives that never get standardized into the actual process.
Treating improvement as a project with an end date instead of an ongoing capability.

maturityProgression.name: Reactive
maturityProgression.description: Improvement happens by whether it feels better, with no real baseline.

maturityProgression.name: Repeatable
maturityProgression.description: Improvement happens informally, based on anecdotes, in occasional bursts.

maturityProgression.name: Defined
maturityProgression.description: Improvement work runs against a defined baseline measurement.

maturityProgression.name: Managed
maturityProgression.description: Changes are measured against baseline, with a clear decision to standardize or roll back.

maturityProgression.name: Adaptive
maturityProgression.description: Improvement runs continuously, with experiments run deliberately and results fed back into the system.

whatBreaksWhenWeak: Real improvements can't be distinguished from noise or seasonal variation.
Past gains quietly erode because nothing was standardized to hold them in place.
Improvement effort concentrates on whichever problem is most visible right now, not the most costly one.
The organization repeats the same class of fix without ever confirming it worked.
resources.whenToUse: For any process or system worth investing improvement effort in over time, not just once.
resources.whenNotToUse: Not needed for a process that's about to be retired or replaced entirely.
howToBuild: Establish a measured baseline before proposing or claiming any improvement.
Test changes at a limited scale before full rollout where possible.
Decide explicitly, based on the data, whether to standardize or roll back a change.
Lock in gains by updating the standard, not just by hoping the change sticks.
howToGovern: Require any claimed improvement to reference the baseline it's being measured against.
Periodically check that past improvements haven't quietly eroded.
howToMeasure: Number of improvements with a documented baseline and outcome.
Rate at which past improvements hold versus erode over time.
Time between identifying an opportunity and testing a change.
operatorQuestions: What was the baseline before we called this an improvement?
How will we know if this change actually worked, three months from now?
What prevents this improvement from quietly eroding after the project ends?

investigate: Pick a recent "improvement" and ask what the baseline measurement was before it started.
Check whether a past improvement's gains are still holding today.
evidence: Before-and-after data for recent improvement claims.
Standards or documentation updated (or not) after a past change.
Backlog of proposed improvements and their stated rationale.
observe: Whether improvement work is measured or just felt.
Whether gains from past initiatives are still visible in current performance.
measure: Percentage of improvements with a documented baseline.
Erosion rate of past improvements over time.
doNotYet: Don't declare success without a baseline to compare against.
Don't launch a new improvement initiative before checking if a past one already addressed this.

healthy: A recent improvement can be shown against its baseline with real data.
warning: A past improvement's gains have started slipping and nobody has noticed yet.
failure: Improvement is discussed entirely in terms of how things feel, with no baseline in sight.

resources.title: Governance
resources.question: What keeps a standard, once defined, from quietly stopping being true?
resources.whatItIs: The set of mechanisms that keep standards, decisions, and controls functioning over time — the difference between defining something once and it staying true.
resources.whyThisExists: Documentation captures a moment in time. Nothing about writing a standard down keeps it enforced as the business changes around it — that ongoing enforcement is governance's job, and it doesn't happen by itself.
resources.whyItMatters: Standardization without governance decays. Documentation captures a moment in time; governance is what keeps that moment relevant as the business changes around it.
resources.goodLooksLike: There are clear review cadences, ownership, and escalation paths for every standard and control that matters, and gaps get caught before they become incidents.
resources.badLooksLike: Standards exist because someone wrote them down once, years ago, and nobody has been assigned to keep them current.
failureSymptoms: Standards exist on paper but are inconsistently followed in practice.
No one is responsible for noticing when a control quietly stops working.
Reviews happen, if at all, only after something has already gone wrong.
A policy is cited that nobody has actually verified is still accurate.
commonFailureModes: Writing a new policy without assigning someone to keep it alive.
Adding a governance meeting without giving it real authority to act.
Treating a policy document as equivalent to an active governance mechanism.

maturityProgression.name: Reactive
maturityProgression.description: Governance is informal or absent; standards drift without anyone noticing.

maturityProgression.name: Repeatable
maturityProgression.description: Some review happens, but inconsistently, and without clear ownership.

maturityProgression.name: Defined
maturityProgression.description: Review cadences, ownership, and escalation paths are explicitly defined for key standards.

maturityProgression.name: Managed
maturityProgression.description: Governance gaps and overlaps are actively tracked, and drift is caught before it causes an incident.

maturityProgression.name: Adaptive
maturityProgression.description: Governance mechanisms are tiered by risk and evolve as the standards and controls they protect change.

whatBreaksWhenWeak: Standards decay silently until an incident reveals they were never actually being followed.
Nobody notices a control has stopped working until it fails to catch something costly.
Overlapping governance bodies disagree about who has final say.
Decision rights and process ownership quietly stop matching what's documented.
resources.whenToUse: For any standard, control, or decision process important enough that its decay would be costly.
resources.whenNotToUse: Overkill for a low-stakes, easily reversible standard where informal review is proportional to the risk.
howToBuild: For each important standard or control, name an owner accountable for keeping it current.
Set an explicit review cadence, independent of whether anything has gone wrong recently.
Define an escalation path for when a gap or drift is found.
Tier governance rigor by the cost of failure, not applied uniformly everywhere.
howToGovern: Periodically audit whether documented governance mechanisms are actually being exercised.
Resolve overlapping governance bodies by naming one with final authority.
howToMeasure: Time since each key standard was last actively reviewed.
Number of standards with no assigned owner.
Gaps found through active review versus discovered through an incident.
operatorQuestions: Who is responsible for noticing when this standard stops being followed?
What review cadence keeps this control from quietly decaying?
Where do we have governance on paper but no one actually exercising it?

investigate: Pick a standard that matters and ask who last actively reviewed it, and when.
Check whether a recent incident revealed a control that had quietly stopped working.
evidence: List of key standards or controls and their documented owners.
Review history, if any, for each.
Recent incidents traceable to a governance gap.
observe: Whether standards are cited from memory versus verified as current.
Whether governance forums have real authority or just visibility.
measure: Percentage of standards with a current, active owner.
Time since last review for each key control.
doNotYet: Don't write a new policy before assigning who will keep it alive.
Don't add a governance meeting without giving it actual authority to act.

healthy: A standard's owner can describe when it was last reviewed and what, if anything, changed.
warning: A standard is cited from memory, with nobody confirming it's still accurate.
failure: An incident reveals a control that had silently stopped working, with nobody aware.
